question.text: A put option is Out of the Money (OTM) when:

answer.text: Spot price of the underlying is higher than the strike price
Spot price of the underlying is lower than the strike price
Spot price of the underlying equals the strike price

explanation.text: The Logic: A put option gives the holder the right to sell at the strike price. The put is OTM when the spot price of the underlying is higher than the strike price, because the holder has no incentive to sell at the lower strike when the market price is higher. A call option is OTM in the opposite case, when the spot price is lower than the strike price. When spot equals strike, the option is at-the-money (ATM). The Trap: Saying spot is lower than strike describes a call OTM (or equivalently, a put ITM), not a put OTM. Spot equal to strike is ATM. Option premiums cannot be negative for a live exchange-traded option, so that distractor is incorrect. Note: Rewrote the options and the explanation in plain English (e.g., 'higher than', 'lower than') to avoid raw '<'/'>' characters that previously truncated the explanation when parsed as XML, and removed the cross-exam/pro-tip lines that were not source-grounded.
